title: Europe Backs Zelenskyy's Peace Push to Putin. India's Diplomatic Tightrope Just Got Thinner.
excerpt: Britain, France, and Germany endorse Ukraine's call for direct talks with Russia. With Trump focused on Iran, India is watching both wars at once.
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood alongside the leaders of Britain, France, and Germany in London on Sunday and made something clear: Europe is no longer waiting for Washington to broker peace with Russia. With the United States consumed by the Iran conflict and President Trump's attention fixed on the Strait of Hormuz, Zelenskyy has opened a direct channel to Russian President Vladimir Putin — and Europe has publicly backed him.

In a joint statement from Downing Street, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and French President Emmanuel Macron endorsed Zelenskyy's written proposal to Putin for face-to-face talks. They laid out conditions for negotiations: an immediate ceasefire, legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine including the deployment of a multinational force, and the continued freezing of Russian assets until Moscow compensates Ukraine for war damage.

Putin rejected the offer, saying he saw "no point in meeting" and questioning the sincerity of Zelenskyy's proposal. But the mechanics of the letter — written directly from Zelenskyy to Putin, citing Russian public fatigue with inflation, fuel shortages, and drone attacks — represent a shift in tone. Zelenskyy acknowledged for the first time that the United States may not return its focus to Europe anytime soon, writing that "it would be wrong to simply wait until the war in Europe returns to the centre of its attention."

## Why India Is Watching Closely

India has maintained its position as what Prime Minister Narendra Modi has called "not a neutral bystander, but on the side of peace." But the Ukraine conflict puts Delhi in a permanent balancing act.

India remains one of Russia's largest oil buyers. Russian crude imports hit 1.9 million barrels per day in May — a lifeline at a time when the Hormuz crisis has squeezed Middle Eastern supplies and pushed Brent above $95 a barrel. Any peace deal that lifts Western sanctions on Russia, or at least reshuffles the enforcement regime, could ease pressure on global energy markets and directly benefit India's import bill.

At the same time, India has quietly deepened its ties with Ukraine. Modi visited Kyiv in August 2024 — the highest-profile visit by a leader from a country that has refused to condemn Russia — and spoke with Zelenskyy by phone as recently as August 2025, reaffirming India's support for a diplomatic resolution.

India's calculation has been consistent: maintain access to Russian energy, preserve strategic autonomy, and avoid being drawn into a proxy alignment with either side. But Trump's pivot toward Iran has complicated this. With Washington distracted and Europe stepping into the diplomatic vacuum, India faces questions about whether its balancing act is sustainable — or whether it will be forced to choose sides as the war enters its fifth year.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the 5.4 million Indians in the United States and the growing Indian communities across Europe, the Ukraine conflict is not abstract. It has reshaped energy markets, fueled inflation, and tightened visa and immigration regimes.

Indian professionals working across Europe — particularly in Poland, Germany, and the UK, countries with significant defence and humanitarian commitments to Ukraine — have watched the conflict become part of their daily political environment. European governments are now linking defence spending, which has risen sharply, to immigration and labour policy. Germany's latest immigration reform explicitly ties skilled-worker visa quotas to national security priorities shaped in part by the Ukraine war.

The NRI business community also has skin in the game. Indian IT companies with large European operations have reported higher costs from energy-driven inflation and currency volatility across the eurozone. A ceasefire that stabilises European energy markets would ease margins for the $280 billion Indian IT industry, roughly a third of whose revenue comes from European clients.

## What Comes Next

Putin's rejection of Zelenskyy's letter does not close the door. Trump, despite his focus on Iran, told NBC News on Sunday that he believed an agreement to end the wider Middle East conflict was close. European officials are betting that if a Hormuz deal materialises, Trump will turn his attention back to Ukraine — and they want the groundwork laid.

For India, the next few weeks will test whether its "multi-alignment" foreign policy can hold under pressure from two simultaneous conflicts. The war in Ukraine and the war in the Middle East are no longer separate crises. They share an oil market, an arms trade, and a set of diplomatic players that India cannot afford to alienate. Modi's tightrope has never been thinner.
